items.prompt: A loop creates one click callback per item and every callback reads the loop counter later. Why does declaring the counter with `let` instead of `var` change what the callbacks see?
items.answer: `let` is block-scoped, so each iteration gets its own binding and every callback keeps the value from its own pass
distractors: `let` copies the counter into each callback at creation time, while `var` passes it by reference to the callback
`var` is hoisted to the top of the loop body, so every callback reads `undefined` until the loop finishes
`let` makes the loop run synchronously before any callback is created, so the counter is already final
items.explanation: Problem 8: each `{ }` block is a new scope for let/const, which is why `let` in a for loop gives each iteration its own variable; `var` is function-scoped, so all callbacks share one variable.

items.answer: With no comparator, sort compares the elements as strings, and the string "10" sorts before "5"
distractors: sort is not stable for numbers, so equal-length values keep an arbitrary relative order
sort only orders by the first digit and keeps the original order for any remaining ties
sort uses insertion order for small arrays and only compares numerically above ten elements
items.explanation: Problem 13: the default sort compares as STRINGS; pass `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers and copy first because sort mutates in place.

items.prompt: To delete the todo with id 2 from React-style state, why does the lab use `todos.filter((t) => t.id !== 2)` rather than `splice` on the existing array?
items.answer: filter builds a new array and leaves the original list untouched, which is the update shape React state expects
distractors: filter is faster than splice because it skips the index lookup that splice needs
splice cannot remove items by id, only by value, so it would delete the wrong todo
filter deep-clones every remaining todo, so later edits cannot reach the old objects
items.explanation: Problem 18: add = spread, remove = filter, update = map + spread; none of them mutate the original array. filter copies the array, not the objects inside it.

items.prompt: `debouncedSearch` is called with "j", "ja" and "java" in quick succession (delay 300ms). What happens to the first two calls, and why?
items.answer: Each new call runs clearTimeout on the pending timer before scheduling its own, so only "java" runs, 300ms after the last call
distractors: All three searches run 300ms apart, because each call queues its own timer behind the previous one
Only "j" runs, because the first timer locks out later calls until its 300ms window has ended
All three run together after 300ms, because setTimeout batches callbacks that share one delay
items.explanation: Problem 22: the closure keeps `timerId`; `clearTimeout(timerId)` cancels the pending call and a fresh `setTimeout` schedules a new one.

items.prompt: `timer.start()` passes `function () { console.log(this.seconds); }` to setTimeout and logs undefined. Why does switching the callback to an arrow function fix it?
items.answer: An arrow function has no `this` of its own and inherits it from start(), where `this` is the timer object
distractors: Arrow functions run synchronously inside start(), so they read `seconds` before the timer fires
Arrow functions are automatically bound to the object they are written in, like a class method
setTimeout calls arrow callbacks with the original object as an argument instead of as `this`
items.explanation: Problem 23: `this` is set by how a function is called (the timer machinery calls the plain function); arrows capture `this` lexically. `.bind(this)` is the other fix.

items.prompt: A page loads three users with `await Promise.all([...])` and one request rejects. What does the page get, and which tool keeps the two successful users?
items.answer: Promise.all rejects with that one error and returns no results; Promise.allSettled reports every outcome so the two successes can be kept
distractors: Promise.all resolves with the two users and an undefined slot; allSettled would only add the error message
Promise.all retries the failed request once and then resolves; allSettled skips the retry and rejects
Promise.all waits for all three and then rejects with an array of errors; allSettled would throw sooner
items.explanation: Problem 28: if ANY promise rejects, Promise.all rejects immediately with that error; allSettled returns fulfilled/rejected records you can filter.

items.prompt: Three independent ~200ms requests are written as three consecutive `await fetchUser(n)` lines. What is the cost compared with one `await Promise.all` over the three calls?
items.answer: About 600ms instead of about 200ms, because each await waits for the previous request before the next one even starts
distractors: About the same, because the event loop already runs consecutive awaits in parallel behind the scenes
About 200ms either way, but the consecutive version uses three times the memory while it waits
Faster than Promise.all, because consecutive awaits avoid the overhead of combining three promises
items.explanation: Problem 28: sequential awaits take ~600ms total; starting all three and awaiting the combined promise takes ~200ms. Spotting independent awaits is an easy performance win.

items.prompt: createPost sends `body: JSON.stringify({ title, body, userId: 1 })` with a `Content-Type: application/json` header. Why are both needed?
items.answer: fetch will not serialize a plain object for you, and the header is what tells the server the string it receives is JSON
distractors: JSON.stringify compresses the body for the network, and the header asks the server to decompress it
fetch serializes the object itself, but the header is required before fetch is allowed to send a body
The header makes fetch call JSON.stringify automatically, so writing it out by hand only adds safety
items.explanation: Problem 30: the three things beginners forget are the method, the Content-Type header, and JSON.stringify (fetch won't serialize objects).

items.prompt: updatePost sends only `{ title: "Edited" }`. Why does the lab use PATCH for that request rather than PUT?
items.answer: PATCH means change only the listed fields, while PUT means replace the whole resource with the body that was sent
distractors: PUT is reserved for creating new resources, so it would add a second post instead of editing one
PATCH is idempotent and PUT is not, so retrying a PUT could apply the title change twice
PUT cannot carry a JSON body, so the title would have to be moved into the query string
items.explanation: Problem 31: PATCH = change only these fields; PUT = replace the whole resource. CRUD: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PUT/PATCH, Delete=DELETE.

items.prompt: In fetchWithRetry, what would the caller observe if the final `throw lastError;` were deleted and every attempt failed?
items.answer: The function would resolve with undefined, so the caller's .then runs with no data and its .catch never fires
distractors: The loop would retry forever, because nothing would stop it once the attempts were used up
The last error would still reach .catch, because the catch block inside the loop already rethrows it
Node would crash with an unhandled rejection, because the errors were caught but never logged
items.explanation: Problem 32: the catch inside the loop swallows each failure (lastError = err); `throw lastError` after the loop is what surfaces the final error once all attempts are exhausted.

items.prompt: `{ date: new Date(), fn: () => 1, missing: undefined }` is saved with JSON.stringify and read back with JSON.parse. What comes back?
items.answer: Only `date`, now an ISO string rather than a Date; the function and the undefined field are dropped
distractors: All three keys, with `fn` turned into its source text and `missing` turned into null
An exact copy, because JSON.parse rebuilds Date objects and functions from their type tags
Nothing at all, because JSON.stringify throws when an object contains a function value
items.explanation: Problem 36 bonus: the JSON round trip loses things; Date became a string and functions/undefined were dropped.

items.prompt: In the task store, `update` throws NotFoundError for an unknown id but `remove` only returns a boolean. What is the design reasoning for remove?
items.answer: Returning false reports that nothing was deleted and lets the caller decide whether a missing id is actually an error
distractors: remove cannot throw because filter swallows any exception raised inside its callback
Returning false is faster than throwing, and deletion is the hottest path in a CRUD store
remove re-inserts the task when it returns false, so callers can retry the delete safely
items.explanation: Problem 46: `return tasks.length < before; // false = nothing deleted; caller decides if that's an error`.

items.prompt: toggleTodoOptimistic keeps `const original = todos` and renders it again when saveFn fails. Why would rollback break if the toggle flipped `t.done` in place instead of using map + spread?
items.answer: `original` points at the same objects, so an in-place flip would change it too and the rollback would render the flipped state
distractors: The in-place flip would make saveFn run twice, so the server would receive the toggle a second time
render() only re-draws when it receives a new array reference, so the rollback would be skipped
The catch block would never run, because mutating an array cancels the pending saveFn promise
items.explanation: Problem 49: immutability makes the rollback trivial; the old array still exists untouched because it was never mutated.

items.prompt: createStore's getAll() returns `[...tasks]`. What could a caller do if it returned the private `tasks` array itself?
items.answer: Push or splice the store's private array directly, adding tasks that never went through add()'s validation
distractors: Nothing harmful, because the closure makes the array read-only to any code outside createStore
Read tasks only after the next add(), because the closure hands out a stale snapshot of the array
Change task ids freely, because returning the array also exposes the private nextId counter
items.explanation: Problem 45: the array is private via closure, and getAll returns a copy so callers can't mutate the store's state; add() validates and trims input.

items.front: Settings code reads `const pageSize = settings.pageSize || 10;` and a user has saved `pageSize: 0`. What does the app use, and why?
items.back: It uses 10: 0 is falsy, so || discards the user's value. Fix: `settings.pageSize ?? 10`, which falls back only on null/undefined. Keep || for real boolean logic.

items.front: Code copies a profile with `const shallow = { ...original }` and then sets `shallow.address.city = "NYC"`. A bug report says the original profile's city changed too. Why?
items.back: Spread copies one level; `address` is a shared nested object, so the write lands in both. Fix: `structuredClone(original)` (or copy the nested level too) when the copy must be independent.

items.front: A getTodo helper does `const res = await fetch(url); return res.json();` with a .catch on the caller. For a missing id the server answers 404, yet the catch never fires. Why?
items.back: fetch only rejects on network failure; a 404/500 still resolves. Without `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...)` the error body is parsed as data. Fix: check res.ok before res.json().

items.front: A deletePost helper ends with `return res.json();` after a DELETE. Deletes succeed on the server but the UI shows an error every time. What is happening?
items.back: DELETE often returns 204 No Content; parsing an empty body as JSON throws, turning a successful delete into a failure. Fix: check res.ok and do not parse the body of a DELETE (or check for 204 first).
